passage: Two weeks after the new handover rules began, Avni booked ten minutes with each of the two in the glass meeting room. Sonali went first. "The rules help, but the note takes me forty minutes and nobody reads to the end." Then Vishal said the same thing in different words: too long. Avni looked at the template on the screen. It had nine headings. Together they cut it down to three: changed, pending, contact. Both nodded. "I'll ask again next month," Avni said, and put a fifteen-minute slot in the calendar for the first Friday of each month. Sonali left the room looking lighter, and Vishal was already opening the shorter template.

qa.a: Sonali felt lighter and relieved, since the note would no longer take forty minutes.

qa.a: Avni could ask whether anyone reads the shortened notes and change the format again if not, because a rule should be adjusted until it serves the people using it.

qa.a: Vishal probably felt listened to and glad the complaint led to a quick change, since Vishal was already opening the shorter template.

grounding: Illustrates a lead checking after two weeks how new working rules are going, shortening a too-long handover note and keeping a short monthly check-in.

Subject: Two weeks in — how's the handover working?

Hi Ayesha,

It's been two weeks since you and Bhavesh started the new handover note between the morning and night shifts at the lab. I asked Bhavesh the same question yesterday, and now I'd like your honest view too.

He told me the note is useful but takes almost twenty minutes to fill in, so he sometimes skips parts. If you're finding the same, let's cut it down. I'm thinking just three boxes: samples pending, machines needing attention, anything urgent.

Could you tell me by Friday which parts you actually read? After that, I'd like to keep a quick fifteen-minute check-in with each of you on the first Monday of every month, just to see it's still working.

Thanks for sticking with this.

Deepika

qa.q: How long did Bhavesh say the note takes to fill in?
qa.a: He said it takes almost twenty minutes to fill in.

qa.q: What does Deepika's email suggest Deepika wants from Ayesha?
qa.a: Deepika seems eager for an honest opinion and a little concerned the note has become a chore, hoping Ayesha will say which parts truly help.

qa.q: What else could Deepika try if shortening the note still didn't work?
qa.a: Deepika could bring Ayesha and Bhavesh together for a short talk about the handover itself, so they design the note together.

qa.q: How is Bhavesh affected by Deepika's check-in?
qa.a: His complaint about the long note is taken seriously, so he can expect a shorter form and may feel less pressured to skip parts.

grounding: It shows a lead checking in two weeks later, finding the handover note too long, shortening it and setting a short monthly check-in.

So you asked how the fight between my two data engineers ended, Elizabeth? Honestly, it's still a work in progress, but it's better.
You remember the rules we set: a clear owner for each pipeline and a handover note every evening. I thought that was the fix. Two weeks later I sat with Rafi, then with Mei Lin, separately, and just asked, "How's it going?"
Both said the same thing. The handover note was a monster. Fifteen fields. Mei Lin admitted she'd stopped filling half of it by day four.
I felt a bit silly, to be honest. I'd built something so thorough that nobody used it.
So we cut it to four fields. And now I have a ten-minute check-in with each of them on the last Friday of every month. That's it. Me, Gurpreet, running a monthly chai meeting like my old boss did.

qa.q: How many fields did the handover note have before it was cut?
How did Gurpreet feel on learning the handover note was too long?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt a bit silly and humbled, having built something so thorough that nobody used it.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet add to make the arrangement last?
qa.a: Gurpreet could ask Rafi and Mei Lin to suggest changes to the four fields at each monthly check-in, so the note keeps fitting their work.

qa.q: How might Mei Lin see the change after the check-in?
qa.a: Mei Lin probably feels relieved and listened to, because the monster form she had quietly stopped using is now short enough to fill in.

grounding: It shows a lead checking in after two weeks, learning the handover note is too long, shortening it and keeping a short monthly check-in.
